title: Concept map: moral hazard, for the Scott Nelson portfolio
timezone_note: Dates in this file are calendar dates. The work was done in America/Los_Angeles.

nodes.label: Moral hazard
nodes.summary: Hidden action after (or because of) a risk-transfer contract. Insurance, or another guarantee, changes the insured party's incentives, so the loss probability or the loss size is not the same as it would have been without coverage. Pauly (1968) argued that this is ordinary price theory, not a moral failing. Arrow (1968) accepted the incentive point and kept a residual role for professional and social norms.

nodes.label: Arrow 1963: uncertainty and medical care
nodes.summary: Arrow compared medical care with the competitive welfare benchmark and traced many of its special features to uncertainty in both the incidence of illness and the efficacy of treatment. He argued that the welfare case for insurance is strong, and that missing insurance markets are a form of market failure. This paper is the origin of the modern economic discussion, even though 'moral hazard' is treated more fully in the 1968 exchange.

nodes.label: Pauly 1968: comment
nodes.summary: A reply to Arrow (1963). If demand for medical care is price-elastic, insurance that lowers the out-of-pocket price raises use. Full coverage need not be optimal, and the absence of some insurance markets need not imply that government should supply the missing cover. The response is rational economic behavior.

nodes.label: Arrow 1968: further comment
nodes.summary: Arrow accepted Pauly's claim that complete insurance is no longer optimal when the insurance method itself influences demand. He likened the incentive effect to an excise tax. He also argued that Pauly's exclusive emphasis on market incentives overlooked norms and self-imposed constraints that can limit the response.

nodes.label: Ex ante moral hazard
nodes.summary: A change in preventive effort, or in other actions taken before a loss, that shifts the probability (or the distribution) of the loss. Ehrlich and Becker (1972) separate market insurance, self-insurance (reducing the size of a loss), and self-protection (reducing its probability). Zweifel and Manning (2000) report that theory does not unambiguously predict a fall in prevention, and that empirical evidence on ex ante moral hazard in health care is limited.

nodes.label: Ex post moral hazard
nodes.summary: A change in the amount or intensity of the loss, or in the use of a covered service, after a loss or illness has occurred. In health insurance this is the rise in medical-care use when the out-of-pocket price falls. Zweifel and Manning (2000) treat static ex post moral hazard as the case with the stronger theory and the stronger evidence, and they also flag a possible dynamic form (bias toward new, costlier technology).

nodes.label: Hidden-action principal-agent model
nodes.summary: A principal writes a contract on an observed outcome. The agent chooses an unobserved action (effort) that shifts the distribution of that outcome. The tension is risk-sharing versus incentives: a risk-averse agent would like to be insulated from luck, but insulation dulls effort.

nodes.label: Informativeness principle (Holmström 1979)
nodes.summary: A signal other than the outcome should be written into the contract if and only if it carries information about the hidden action that the outcome does not already contain. This is the contract-design cousin of the value of information on the decision-theory page.

nodes.label: Grossman-Hart 1983 two-stage approach
nodes.summary: Because the first-order approach to the agent's incentive constraint is not generally valid (a point associated with Mirrlees), Grossman and Hart split the problem: first find the cheapest contract that implements a given action, then choose the action. This is the standard way to characterize optimal incentive schemes.

nodes.label: Holmström-Milgrom 1987 linear contracts
nodes.summary: In a continuous-time model with exponential utility and Brownian information, the optimal incentive scheme is linear in aggregated outcomes. This is the usual justification for studying simple linear sharing rules (including coinsurance) rather than highly nonlinear contracts.

nodes.label: Holmström-Milgrom 1991 multitasking
nodes.summary: When the agent has several tasks and some are harder to measure than others, strong incentives on the measurable task can pull effort away from the unmeasurable one (for example, quality, prevention, or long-term care). Incentive intensity should fall when measurement is unbalanced.

nodes.label: Adverse selection (hidden type)
nodes.summary: Hidden information about risk type, not hidden action. Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976) show that a competitive insurance market with hidden types may have a separating equilibrium in which higher-risk agents buy more coverage, or may have no equilibrium. This is the other information problem in insurance, and it is what the actuarial page names as 'anti-selection' when it appears as a loading.

nodes.label: Positive-correlation test
nodes.summary: Chiappori and Salanié (2000) test for a positive correlation between coverage and claims, conditional on observables. A positive residual correlation is evidence of asymmetric information, but it does not by itself say whether the cause is adverse selection, moral hazard, or both. Their French automobile data did not reject the null of no residual correlation in that sample.

nodes.label: Separating selection from moral hazard
nodes.summary: Einav, Finkelstein, and Cullen (2010) use price variation to trace demand and average-cost curves and to measure the welfare cost of selection. Einav, Finkelstein, Ryan, Schrimpf, and Cullen (2013) go further and estimate selection on moral hazard: people who choose more coverage also have a larger behavioral response to coverage. Both papers use confidential employer data, not a public file.

nodes.label: RAND Health Insurance Experiment
nodes.summary: Families were randomly assigned to plans with different cost sharing, which identifies a price response without confounding by plan choice. Manning, Newhouse, Duan, Keeler, Leibowitz, and Marquis (1987) report that a catastrophic plan reduces expenditures 31 percent relative to a zero out-of-pocket price, and that the price elasticity is approximately 0.2 in absolute value. Aron-Dine, Einav, and Finkelstein (2013) review the design and the later re-analyses. Public-use microdata are at ICPSR 6439.

nodes.label: Oregon Health Insurance Experiment
nodes.summary: A 2008 lottery for a limited number of Medicaid slots. Finkelstein, Taubman, Wright, Bernstein, Gruber, Newhouse, Allen, Baicker, and the Oregon Health Study Group (2012) study the first year. The lottery provides random variation in coverage, so utilization differences are not an artifact of who chose to buy insurance. Public-use data and replication code are on the NBER Oregon page, under click-through terms.

nodes.label: Deductibles
nodes.summary: The insured pays the first dollars of a loss. Mossin (1968) shows that when insurance is loaded above the actuarial premium, a positive deductible is optimal for a risk-averse buyer. Raviv (1979) studies the broader design of an optimal policy. On the applied page, the deductible is already the residual D in p* = C/(L-D), but p does not respond to D.

nodes.label: Coinsurance and copays
nodes.summary: A sharing rule: the insured pays a fraction of the loss, or a fixed copay per use. Zeckhauser (1970) is the classic analysis of the tradeoff between risk spreading and incentives in medical insurance. Linear coinsurance is also the applied form of the Holmström-Milgrom 1987 linear contract. The applied page lists a copay as one reading of D, and does not mention coinsurance by name.

nodes.label: Experience rating and bonus-malus
nodes.summary: Future premiums depend on past claims. This is both a statistical shrinkage problem (Bühlmann credibility on the actuarial page) and an incentive device: the insured internalizes part of the future cost of a claim. Bonus-malus and no-claims discounts in motor insurance are the usual examples. Shavell (1979) analyzes observation of care and the use of such instruments under moral hazard.

nodes.label: Monitoring and telematics
nodes.summary: A direct application of the informativeness principle: if a signal of hidden action can be observed, it belongs in the contract. In automobile insurance this includes mileage and telematic driving data. Edlin (1999) analyzes per-mile premiums as a way to price the marginal mile. Usage-based insurance is the later commercial form of the same idea.

nodes.label: Health insurance
nodes.summary: The setting of Arrow, Pauly, Zeckhauser, the RAND experiment, the Oregon experiment, and the Einav-Finkelstein program. Ex post utilization responses are the best-documented form of moral hazard in this domain. Ex ante prevention responses are weaker and less settled (Zweifel and Manning 2000).

nodes.label: Automobile insurance
nodes.summary: The main field for bonus-malus, experience rating, and telematics, and the setting of the Chiappori-Salanié (2000) test. The Peltzman (1975) offset hypothesis, that safety regulation can induce more risk-taking, is a related risk-compensation mechanism, not itself an insurance-contract result.

nodes.label: Deposit insurance, too-big-to-fail, and bailouts
nodes.summary: A fixed-rate guarantee of bank liabilities can encourage risk-taking. Keeley (1990) links this moral hazard to the decline of bank charter values and to later problems in the 1980s. Farhi and Tirole (2012) study collective moral hazard when private leverage choices anticipate a systemic bailout. The page should keep this as a mechanism and evidence discussion, not a political argument.

nodes.label: Unemployment insurance
nodes.summary: The cleanest applied decision-theory statement of the insurance-incentive tradeoff is the Baily-Chetty formula: the optimal benefit balances the consumption-smoothing gain (risk aversion times the consumption drop) against the moral-hazard cost (the elasticity of unemployment duration with respect to benefits). Chetty (2006) generalizes Baily (1978). Chetty (2008) separates moral hazard from liquidity effects in the duration response.

nodes.label: Disaster insurance
nodes.summary: Flood and catastrophe insurance raise both ordinary moral hazard (less mitigation when losses are covered) and a related 'charity hazard': expected public relief can crowd out private insurance (Raschky and Weck-Hannemann 2007). Browne and Hoyt (2000) study demand for cover under the U.S. National Flood Insurance Program, including the role of previous disaster relief.

nodes.label: Peltzman effect / risk compensation
nodes.summary: Peltzman (1975) argued that automobile safety regulation can be offset, in part, by more aggressive driving. This is risk compensation: a reduction in the expected cost of an accident changes behavior. It is included on the map as a cousin of ex ante moral hazard, not as a result about insurance contracts.

nodes.label: Expected utility and risk aversion
nodes.summary: The buyer's reason to want insurance. Pratt (1964) defines the Arrow-Pratt coefficients of risk aversion. The applied insurance thread already uses the approximation (1/2) A(W) Var(loss) for the risk premium, without naming the source. The actuarial page uses an insurer risk-aversion coefficient in the exponential premium principle.

nodes.label: Optimal-insurance tradeoff and the Baily-Chetty formula
nodes.summary: Insurance has value because it smooths consumption, and a cost because it changes behavior. At the optimum, those two forces balance. Zeckhauser (1970) and Mossin (1968) are the insurance-contract versions. Baily (1978) and Chetty (2006) give the social-insurance version, often called the Baily-Chetty formula. Chetty's equation (8) equates the gap in marginal utilities between the unemployed and employed states to the elasticity term (b/D)(dD/db). The first-order (quadratic-utility) approximation is Baily's inverse-elasticity rule. This draft does not restate a compact typographic form of that approximation, because PDF text extraction garbled the symbols. Any page formula should be copied from the typeset papers, not from this file.

nodes.label: Portfolio: applied decision theory
nodes.summary: Existing playground. Insurance thread and break-even calculator treat p as fixed. Natural place to extend D so that p or L depends on coverage.

nodes.label: Portfolio: actuarial pricing
nodes.summary: Existing pricing track. Loadings already name an anti-selection margin. Credibility already names experience rating and bonus-malus. Neither is modeled as a hidden-action remedy.

nodes.label: Portfolio: decision-theory ladder
nodes.summary: Existing curriculum for expected utility, MEU, and VPI. Supplies the buyer's objective and the information-value language that the informativeness principle echoes.
